about: Strong and weak gravity near any mass (exotic objects design, track XO, package XO1): sizes, bending, clocks and tides. The bend table itself is a kernel table in crates/sse-gravity.

references: Schwarzschild, K. 1916, Über das Gravitationsfeld eines Massenpunktes nach der Einsteinschen Theorie, Sitzungsber. Preuss. Akad. Wiss., 189 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1916SPAW.......189S
Misner, C. W., Thorne, K. S. and Wheeler, J. A. 1973, Gravitation, W. H. Freeman (Schwarzschild geometry, chapters 25 and 31) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973grav.book.....M

equation.name: The length that sets the size of everything strong gravity does

source.text: Schwarzschild 1916; Misner, Thorne and Wheeler 1973, Gravitation

explain.curious: Every mass has a length of its own. For the Sun it is about 1.5 km, for the Earth about 4.4 mm. Strong gravity happens within a few of these lengths: a black hole's edge is two of them from the middle.
explain.science: r_g = GM/c². Every distance in the Schwarzschild and Kerr geometries scales with it: horizon 2 r_g (no spin), photon orbit 3 r_g, last stable orbit 6 r_g, shadow √27 r_g.

references: Kerr, R. P. 1963, Gravitational field of a spinning mass as an example of algebraically special metrics, Phys. Rev. Lett. 11, 237. doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.11.237
Misner, C. W., Thorne, K. S. and Wheeler, J. A. 1973, Gravitation, W. H. Freeman (Schwarzschild geometry, chapters 25 and 31) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973grav.book.....M

a.name: spin a = Jc/GM², signed: below zero means against the spin

rh.name: radius of the surface of no return

source.where: outer horizon of the Kerr metric in Boyer-Lindquist coordinates

explain.curious: Inside this surface not even light gets out. A black hole of ten Suns is 60 km across. Spinning shrinks it, to half at the fastest spin.
explain.science: Outer horizon r₊ = M + √(M² − a²) (G = c = 1): 2 r_g for no spin, r_g at a = 1. The sign of a does not matter here.

references: Bardeen, J. M. 1973, Timelike and null geodesics in the Kerr metric, in Black Holes (Les Houches 1972), eds. DeWitt and DeWitt, Gordon and Breach, 215 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973blho.conf..215B

Bardeen, J. M., Press, W. H. and Teukolsky, S. A. 1972, Rotating black holes: locally nonrotating frames, energy extraction, and scalar synchrotron radiation, ApJ 178, 347, equations 2.18 to 2.21. doi:10.1086/151796
Luminet, J.-P. 1979, Image of a spherical black hole with thin accretion disk, A&A 75, 228 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1979A%26A....75..228L

equation.name: Where light can go round in a circle
equation.formula:
x = -a
acx = atan2(sqrt(max(1 - x^2, 0)), x)
rph = 2 * rg * (1 + cos(2 / 3 * acx))

a.name: spin a, signed: above zero means light circling with the spin

rph.name: radius of the circular orbit of light in the equator

explain.curious: Light passing at just this distance goes round and round. It is the thin bright ring hugging a black hole's shadow.
explain.science: Circular photon orbit in the equatorial plane of a Kerr hole: r = 2M{1 + cos[⅔ arccos(∓a)]}, 3 r_g for no spin, r_g (with the spin) to 4 r_g (against it) at a = 1.

references: Bardeen, J. M., Press, W. H. and Teukolsky, S. A. 1972, Rotating black holes: locally nonrotating frames, energy extraction, and scalar synchrotron radiation, ApJ 178, 347, equations 2.18 to 2.21. doi:10.1086/151796

equation.name: The innermost orbit matter can keep
equation.formula:
s = abs(a)
z1 = 1 + cbrt(1 - s^2) * (cbrt(1 + s) + cbrt(1 - s))
z2 = sqrt(3 * s^2 + z1^2)
d = sqrt(max((3 - z1) * (3 + z1 + 2 * z2), 0))
risco = if a < 0 then rg * (3 + z2 + d) else rg * (3 + z2 - d)

a.name: spin a, signed: above zero means orbiting with the spin

risco.name: radius of the last stable circular orbit

explain.curious: Closer than this, nothing can orbit for long: gas spirals straight in. It is the inner edge of a black hole's disc, six gravitational radii out with no spin, much closer for a fast spinner.
explain.science: Marginally stable circular orbit of the Kerr metric (Bardeen, Press and Teukolsky 1972, eq. 2.21): 6 r_g at a = 0, 1.237 r_g at a = 0.998 prograde, 9 r_g at a = 1 retrograde. The sign choice is a real boundary (the orbit's direction), not a class.

references: Synge, J. L. 1966, The escape of photons from gravitationally intense stars, MNRAS 131, 463 (angular size of the capture cone for a static observer). doi:10.1093/mnras/131.3.463

equation.name: How big the dark middle looks from here
equation.formula:
q = rg / D
sn = if D <= 3 * rg then 1 else sqrt(27) * q * sqrt(1 - 2 * q)
theta = atan2(sn, sqrt(max(1 - sn^2, 0)))

D.name: distance of the viewer from the hole's centre

theta.name: angular radius of the shadow, radians

source.where: capture cone of a static observer

explain.curious: A black hole's shadow is two and a half times wider than the hole itself, because light that passes too close is swallowed. M87's looks 40 millionths of an arcsecond across from here.
explain.science: For a viewer at rest at radius D outside a non-spinning hole, sin θ = √27 (M/D)(1 − 2M/D)^½; far away the shadow's edge has impact parameter √27 M. Spin changes the size by up to about 4% and flattens one side (not in this block; see the fudge register). Inside the photon orbit (D ≤ 3M) the dark part covers more than half the sky; this block stops at 90°.

references: Einstein, A. 1915, Erklärung der Perihelbewegung des Merkur aus der allgemeinen Relativitätstheorie, Sitzungsber. Preuss. Akad. Wiss., 831 (light deflection 4GM/c²b) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1915SPAW.......831E
Dyson, F. W., Eddington, A. S. and Davidson, C. 1920, A determination of the deflection of light by the Sun's gravitational field, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. A 220, 291. doi:10.1098/rsta.1920.0009

equation.name: How much a mass bends light passing at a distance

b.name: distance at which the light passes the mass

alpha.name: angle the light is turned, radians

explain.curious: Light grazing the Sun is turned by 1.75 seconds of arc, as Eddington's eclipse team measured in 1919. Far from any mass this one line is all the bending there is.
explain.science: First-order deflection α = 4GM/(c²b), good when b ≫ r_g (the next term is 15π/4 (r_g/b)², 6% at b = 50 r_g). Closer in, the bend table takes over.

references: Einstein, A. 1936, Lens-like action of a star by the deviation of light in the gravitational field, Science 84, 506. doi:10.1126/science.84.2188.506

equation.name: The ring a star makes behind a mass

Ds.name: distance to the light behind it

thetaE.name: angular radius of the Einstein ring, radians

explain.curious: A star exactly behind a mass is drawn out into a ring. Slightly off, it makes two images, one each side; this is the size they sit at.
explain.science: Point-lens Einstein radius with flat-space distances, D_ls = D_s − D_l. Across a galaxy that is exact enough; across the universe the distances become angular-diameter distances (not in this block).

references: Misner, C. W., Thorne, K. S. and Wheeler, J. A. 1973, Gravitation, W. H. Freeman (Schwarzschild geometry, chapters 25 and 31) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973grav.book.....M
Schwarzschild, K. 1916, Über das Gravitationsfeld eines Massenpunktes nach der Einsteinschen Theorie, Sitzungsber. Preuss. Akad. Wiss., 189 https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1916SPAW.......189S
atoms.shown: dτ/dt = √(1 − 2r_g/r) hovering, √(1 − 3r_g/r) on a circular orbit

equation.name: How slowly a clock runs near a mass
equation.formula:
hover = if r <= 2 * rg then 0 else sqrt(1 - 2 * rg / r)
orbit = if r <= 3 * rg then 0 else sqrt(1 - 3 * rg / r)

hover.name: clock rate against a far clock, holding still

orbit.name: clock rate against a far clock, on a circular orbit

source.where: Schwarzschild metric, static and circular-orbit observers

explain.curious: Near a black hole time runs slow. Holding still at three times the hole's own radius, an hour of yours is about 1 hour 13 minutes far away.
explain.science: Static observer: dτ/dt = (1 − 2M/r)^½; circular geodesic orbit: (1 − 3M/r)^½, gravity and speed together. No circular orbit exists inside 3M (rate 0 means none); a hovering ship there needs a huge thrust.

references: Misner, C. W., Thorne, K. S. and Wheeler, J. A. 1973, Gravitation, W. H. Freeman (Schwarzschild geometry, chapters 25 and 31) https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1973grav.book.....M

equation.name: How hard a mass stretches something along its length

k.name: difference in pull per metre of length

source.where: Newtonian tidal tensor along the radius

explain.curious: Your feet are pulled harder than your head. A thousand km from a black hole of ten Suns the difference over two metres is about five thousand times Earth's gravity; a supermassive hole is gentle by comparison.
explain.science: Radial tidal acceleration per unit length, 2GM/r³ (the radial eigenvalue of the Newtonian tidal tensor; the same in Schwarzschild for a static observer). Multiply by a length for the stretch across it.
